L41: # Superintegrable cellular automata and dual unitary gates from Yang-Baxter maps
L42: 
L43: Tamás Gombor Affiliation: MTA-ELTE “Momentum” Integrable Quantum Dynamics Research Group, Department of Theoretical Physics, Eötvös Loránd University    Balázs Pozsgay Affiliation: MTA-ELTE “Momentum” Integrable Quantum Dynamics Research Group, Department of Theoretical Physics, Eötvös Loránd University
L44: ###### Abstract
L45: We consider one dimensional block cellular automata, where the local update rules are given by Yang-Baxter maps, which are set theoretical solutions of the Yang-Baxter equations. We show that such systems are superintegrable: they possess an exponentially large set of conserved local charges, such that the charge densities propagate ballistically on the chain. For these quantities we observe a complete absence of “operator spreading”.
L46: In addition, the models can also have other local charges which are conserved only additively. We discuss concrete models up to local dimensions $N\leq 4$, and show that they give rise to rich physical behaviour, including non-trivial scattering of particles and the coexistence of ballistic and diffusive transport. We find that the local update rules are classical versions of the “dual unitary gates” if the Yang-Baxter maps are non-degenerate.
L47: We discuss consequences of dual unitarity, and we also discuss a family of dual unitary gates obtained by a non-integrable quantum mechanical deformation of the Yang-Baxter maps.
L48: ## 1 Introduction
L49: The dynamics of many body interacting models is generally intractable with analytic methods, and this holds true for both classical and quantum models. It is only in specific circumstances that exact solutions can be found, which makes such systems valuable from a theoretical point of view.
L50: One dimensional integrable models form a well studied class of exactly solvable models, having distinctive features such as the existence of a large set of conserved charges and completely elastic and factorized scattering of quasi-particles [cite29†1 , cite30†2 , cite31†3 ]. However, exact solutions can also be found in other circumstances, for example in quantum circuits with dual unitary gates, as we discuss below.
L51: In this paper we consider two special types of dynamical systems: block cellular automata (BCA) and closely related brickwork quantum circuits (also called quantum cellular automata, QCA) in one space dimension. Even though these are relatively simple systems, it is believed that they display many of the important physical features of more generic systems. For recent reviews of QCA see [cite32†4 , cite33†5 ].
L52: We focus on integrable cases in both the classical and quantum setting, and consider models with a specific brickwork structure for the local update rules. Systems of this type have been studied recently as simple models for non-equilibrium dynamics, both in the classical and quantum settings (see for example [cite34†6 , cite35†7 ]; other relevant references will be given later in the text). However, the understanding of integrable cellular automata with finite configuration spaces is not yet satisfying.
L53: Closely related systems, such as classical integrable equations on discrete space-time lattices are well studied [cite36†8 , cite37†9 , cite38†10 , cite39†11 ], and most of the research deals with models with continuous local configuration spaces, such as the complex numbers or some group manifolds.
L54: These systems display the hallmarks of integrability, such as the existence of a set of higher charges and commuting flows (the latter is also known as multi-dimensional consistency or the cube condition), the appearance of Lax matrices and the Yang-Baxter equation in various forms [cite40†12 , cite41†13 , cite42†14 ], and also a constrained algebraic growth of the iterated functions [cite43†15 ]. A new algebraic approach to discrete time integrable models was formulated recently in [cite44†16 ].
L55: In contrast, less is known in those cases when the configuration space is also finite; these models are sometimes called “ultra-discrete” [cite45†17 ]. In specific cases they were well studied, see for example the so-called box-ball systems [cite45†17 ], which can be understood as the ultra-discretization of integrable field equations.
L56: Cellular automata can be viewed as a classical dynamical systems over finite fields, and algebraic and algebro-geometric aspects were studied in [cite46†18 , cite47†19 , cite48†20 , cite49†21 , cite50†22 ].
L57: BCA with Floquet type update rules attracted considerable attention in the last couple of years, both with finite and continuous configuration spaces [cite51†23 , cite52†24 ]. In the finite case the most studied system has been the so-called Rule54 model [cite36†8 , cite53†25 , cite35†7 ], where exact solutions were found for the dynamics despite the model being interacting [cite54†26 , cite55†27 , cite56†28 , cite57†29 ].
L58: Quite surprisingly, despite having perhaps the simplest dynamics among interacting models, the algebraic integrability of the Rule54 model is still not clarified, see [cite58†30 , cite59†31 ]. A new algebraic framework for spin chains and QCA with “medium range interaction” was developed in [cite59†31 ], where it was shown that the closely related Rule150 model is Yang-Baxter integrable with three-site interactions.
L59: This new approach led to other integrable block cellular automata, for example the model of [cite60†32 ] which is the classical version of the folded XXZ model [cite61†33 , cite62†34 ].
L60: These recent developments motivate further research on BCA. There are two main questions. First of all, how can we find and classify all integrable models of this sort, and second, which one of these models is interesting and useful from a physical point of view. In this second respect we mention the paper [cite34†6 ] and subsequent works [cite63†35 , cite64†36 ] which showed that even a relatively simple solvable system can serve as a useful toy model for generic physical behaviour, such as diffusive transport.
L61: In this paper we consider classical BCA where the update rule is given by a so-called Yang-Baxter map: a set theoretical solution of the Yang-Baxter equation, without any spectral parameters. These maps were introduced by Drinfeld in [cite65†37 ] and studied afterwards in detail in the seminal paper [cite66†38 ]. By now the study of Yang-Baxter maps on finite sets grew into a separate topic in mathematics and mathematical physics.
L62: We do not attempt to give a review of this field, instead we refer the reader to the recent work [cite67†39 ] which deals with the enumeration of Yang-Baxter maps up to size $N=10$.
L63: The novelty of our work is that we build BCA from Yang-Baxter maps; apparently this simple construction was not yet explored in the literature. Closely related constructions were studied in [cite68†40 , cite69†41 ], but these works treated translationally invariant quantum spin chains and not the BCA. The model of [cite34†6 ] belongs to the class we are considering, and it is in fact the simplest non-trivial model in this class, as we show in the main text.
L64: Our aim is to explore the consequences of the Yang-Baxter equation on the dynamics of these models, focusing first on the classical examples. These are treated in Sections cite10†3 -cite22†6 after the general introduction of the setup in Section cite7†2 . We find that the models are super-integrable: they possess an exponentially large set of local conservation laws, and this sets them apart from a generic integrable model.
L65: Afterwards we also consider quantum mechanical deformations (Section cite23†7 ), and explain that the models lose their super-integrability, but remain integrable. We should note that conservation laws in cellular automata were already studied some time ago [cite70†42 , cite71†43 ] and also more recently [cite72†44 ], but these works treat the usual CA, and not the integrable BCA. Conserved operators in Clifford quantum CA were investigated in [cite73†45 ].
L66: Studying the classification of the Yang-Baxter maps we immediately encounter the property of non-degeneracy [cite66†38 ]. This can be seen as the classical analog of the “dual unitary” property of two-site quantum gates. Therefore we also explore the overlap between the dual unitary and integrable quantum circuit models.
L67: The dual unitary circuits are quantum BCA, where the two-site gate is a unitary operator when viewed as a generator of translations in both the time and space directions [cite74†46 , cite75†47 , cite76†48 ]. They are solvable models of quantum computation, which can display integrable and chaotic behaviour as well.
L68: A complete parameterization for dual unitary gates is not known beyond local dimension $N=2$, but quite general constructions were published, see for example [cite77†49 ] or formula (51) of [cite78†50 ] (which was suggested by one of the present authors).
L69: In this work we also contribute to the theory of dual unitary models, by establishing a connection with the Yang-Baxter maps in the integrable cases, and by presenting a non-integrable deformation of such gates, thus obtaining a more general family of dual unitary gates (see Section cite24†8 ).
L70: In Section cite25†9 we present our conclusions and some open problems.
L71: ## 2 Models
L72: 
L73: In this work we consider classical and quantum cellular automata in one space dimension. In the classical case we are dealing with block cellular automata, whereas in the quantum case we switch to unitary quantum circuits of the brickwork type (quantum cellular automata). In this Section we review the basic constructions.
L74: First we discuss the classical case. Let $X$ be a finite set with $N$ elements. We interpret $X$ as a local configuration space. A cellular automaton consists of a collection of cells and an update rule. We consider one dimensional systems, and we deal with classical “spin” variables $s_{j}$ with $j=1,2,\dots,L$ that take values from the set $X$. Here $L$ is the length of the system, which is assumed to be an even number, and we will always consider periodic boundary conditions.
L75: A configuration $s=\{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{L}\}$ is an element of $X^{L}\equiv X\times X\times\dots\times X$, and the update rule $\mathcal{V}$ is a map $X^{L}\to X^{L}$. This means that at each iteration we update the configuration as
L76:  | $$s\quad\to\quad\mathcal{V}s.$$  |  | (1)
L77: 
L78: For the identity map we will use the notation 1 throughout this work.
L79: 
L80: In this work we consider information preserving maps, which means that the update rule has to be an invertible map. The property of invertibility is analogous to “phase space conservation” in Hamiltonian mechanics, see the discussion in [cite79†51 ]. Furthermore we will also require time reflection invariance, which is an additional requirement; details will be specified below.
L81: We consider Floquet-type block cellular automata. Specifically we restrict ourselves to two types of strictly local system, which we call $2\to 2$ and $3\to 1$ models. The Floquet rule consist of two steps in both cases: $\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{2}\mathcal{V}_{1}$, and the maps $\mathcal{V}_{1,2}$ are constructed from commuting local maps. For convenience we choose the time coordinate $t$ such that the action of $\mathcal{V}$ corresponds to $t\to t+2$.
L82: In the case of the $2\to 2$ models we deal with a local two-site map $U:X^{2}\to X^{2}$ and build the update rules as
L83: 
L84:  | $$\begin{split}\mathcal{V}_{1}&=U_{L-1,L}\dots U_{3,4}U_{1,2}\\
L85: \mathcal{V}_{2}&=U_{L,1}\dots U_{4,5}U_{2,3}.\\
L86: \end{split}$$  |  | (2)
L87: 
L88: We require time reflection invariance from our models in all cases. This means that the local update moves should be involutive, i.e. $U_{j,j+1}^{2}=1$. For the Floquet update rule this implies
L89:  | $$\mathcal{V}^{-1}=(\mathcal{V}_{2}\mathcal{V}_{1})^{-1}=\mathcal{V}_{1}\mathcal{V}_{2}.$$  |  | (3)
L90: 
L91: In contrast to the $2\to 2$ models the $3\to 1$ models describe time evolution on light cone lattices, and each local update step uses the information from $3$ sites to give a new value to a variable on one site. In most of this work we will focus on the $2\to 2$ models, and we treat the $3\to 1$ models in Section cite22†6 .
L92: We also consider quantum circuits (also called quantum cellular automata, QCA), whose structure follows from an immediate generalization of what was discussed so far. In the quantum case we are dealing with local Hilbert spaces $\mathbb{C}^{N}$ whose basis is indexed by the elements of the finite set $X$. The full Hilbert space of a quantum chain of length $L$ is given by the $L$-fold tensor product of local spaces, and the state of the system is a vector ${\left|\Psi\right\rangle}$ of this Hilbert space.
L93: In analogy with the classical case we are dealing with two-site maps $\hat{U}_{j,j+1}$ which are now quantum gates acting on a pair of local Hilbert spaces. Furthermore, we construct quantum circuits of brickwork type by the immediate generalization of the Floquet rule (cite80†2 ), by replacing classical maps with operators. Thus we obtain the quantum update rule $\hat{\mathcal{V}}$, and at each step the state of the system is changed as
L94:  | $${\left|\Psi\right\rangle}\quad\to\quad\hat{\mathcal{V}}{\left|\Psi\right\rangle}.$$  |  | (4)
L95: 
L96: Every classical update rule can be lifted immediately to a quantum gate, by defining $\hat{U}$ such that it permutes pairs of basis vectors according to the classical map $U$. To be precise:
L97: 
L98:  | $$\hat{U}\left({\left|a\right\rangle}\otimes{\left|b\right\rangle}\right)={\left|c\right\rangle}\otimes{\left|d\right\rangle},\text{ where }(c,d)=U(a,b).$$  |  | (5)
L99: In such a case the resulting quantum circuit is deterministic in the given basis. On the other hand, we will also consider cases where the two-site gate $\hat{U}_{j,j+1}$ produces linear combinations of the local product states, thus it becomes a true quantum gate.
L100: ### 2.1 Examples
L101: 
L102: Here we give two examples for the models that fit into our framework. Both models are classical, and they appeared earlier in the literature.
L103: 
L104: In the case of the classical $2\to 2$ models the simplest one is what we call the permutation model. It is defined for every set $X$ by the permutation map $\mathcal{P}$:
L105: 
L106:  | $$U(a,b)=\mathcal{P}(a,b)\equiv(b,a),\qquad a,b\in X.$$  |  | (6)
L107: The application of the update rule leads to light cone propagation in the model, with the odd/even sub-lattices performing a cyclic shift to the right/left, respectively. An example for time evolution in this model is shown in Figure cite81†1 .
L108: 
L109: (a) Permutation model with $N=2$
L110: 
L111: (b) XXC model with $N=3$
L112: Figure 1: Examples for time evolution in the classical cellular automata. In the plots the vertical direction corresponds to time, and the horizontal to space; the initial condition is given by the uppermost row, and time flows downwards. We plotted both half-steps of the Floquet cycle $\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{2}\mathcal{V}_{1}$, and we use a convention such that the addition of two rows corresponds to $t\to t+2$. This way the speed of propagation in the permutation model is $v=\pm 1$.
L113: In the space direction periodic boundary conditions are applied.
L114: An other example is the XXC model with $N=3$. Labelling the local configuration space as $X=\{1,2,3\}$ the update rule is defined as
L115: 
L116:  | $$U(a,b)=\begin{cases}&(b,a)\text{ if }a=1\text{ or }b=1\\
L117: &(a,b)\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}$$  |  | (7)
L118: This update rule is closely related to the XXC quantum spin chains studied in [cite82†52 ], hence the name. The map $U$ appears at the “rational point” of the $R$-matrices presented in [cite82†52 ]. The update rule was later independently proposed in [cite34†6 ] and the resulting model was further analyzed in [cite63†35 , cite64†36 ]. In these works it was observed that the map $U$ satisfies the set theoretical Yang-Baxter relation (see Section cite10†3 ).
L119: In the XXC model the state $1$ can be interpreted as the “vacuum”, and the two remaining states can be interpreted as particles with an inner degree of freedom, given by two colors. An example for the time evolution in this model is shown in Fig. cite81†1 . If we focus only on the dynamics of the “charge”, i.e. we forget about the colors, then the model is found to be equivalent to the permutation model. The new features come when we add the non-trivial color dynamics.
L120: It can be seen that the particle numbers for the two colors are separately conserved, but the colors do not propagate ballistically, the colors get reflected during scattering. Therefore, the spatial ordering of the colors is conserved during time evolution, while the particles move along the light cones. This color dynamics is typical for the low energy scattering in quantum models with two-color excitations.
L121: The model shows complex transport properties, and a number of exact results for the real time evolution were computed in [cite34†6 , cite63†35 , cite64†36 ].
L122: ### 2.2 Local symmetries and local conservation laws
L123: 
L124: We are interested in models that have a large set of local conservation laws, and sometimes also a finite set of local symmetries. Therefore we discuss these concepts briefly, and introduce the necessary notations. In these discussions we consider only the $2\to 2$ maps, but the generalization to the $3\to 1$ case is obvious.
L125: First we discuss the symmetries and conservation laws in the classical language. The extension to the quantum case follows immediately, by lifting the classical maps to linear operators.
L126: 
L127: Let $S:X\to X$ be a bijection. We say that the model has global symmetry $S$, if
L128: 
L129:  | $$(S\times S)U_{1,2}=U_{1,2}(S\times S).$$  |  | (8)
L130: 
L131: This implies that the global extension of $S$ defined as $S\times S\times\dots\times S$ is a symmetry of the cellular automaton, it commutes with the global update rule $\mathcal{V}$.
L132: It is also useful to discuss symmetries which can be applied locally. A special situation is if the symmetry operation can be applied along a light cone. We say that the symmetry operation $S$ propagates ballistically if
L133: 
L134:  | $$(1\times S)U_{1,2}=U_{1,2}(S\times 1),\quad\text{ and }\quad(S\times 1)U_{1,2}=U_{1,2}(1\times S).$$  |  | (9)
L135: 
L136: This implies that
L137: 
L138:  | $$\mathcal{V}S_{2k-1}=S_{2k+1}\mathcal{V},\qquad\mathcal{V}S_{2k}=S_{2k-2}\mathcal{V}$$  |  | (10)
L139: for every integer $k$, and we used the notation that $S_{j}$ acts on site $j$. Consecutive application of the relations above implies that the permutation symmetry “propagates along light cones” and it connects different orbits by changing the local states only along a specific light cone.
L140: Let us also discuss conserved charges. We consider functions $q^{(\alpha)}:X^{\alpha}\to\mathbb{Z}$ with $\alpha=1,2,\dots$ and interpret them as local charge densities with range $\alpha$. We chose the image space of the charges to be the integers, which is very natural in systems with finite configuration spaces.
L141: 
L142: Correspondingly, we define translationally invariant extensive charges $Q^{(\alpha)}:X^{L}\to\mathbb{Z}$ as
L143: 
L144:  | $$Q^{(\alpha)}=\sum_{j=1}^{L}q^{(\alpha)}(j),$$  |  | (11)
L145: where it is understood that $q^{(\alpha)}(j)$ is the function $q^{(\alpha)}$ applied on the segment $[j,j+1,\dots,j+\alpha-1]$ of the automaton, and periodic boundary conditions are understood. Our update rules $\mathcal{V}$ are invariant with respect to translation by two sites only, therefore it is useful to study charges with the same invariance properties. This leads to the combinations
L146:  | $$Q^{(\alpha),+}=\sum_{j=1}^{L/2}q^{(\alpha)}(2j+1),\qquad Q^{(\alpha),-}=\sum_{j=1}^{L/2}q^{(\alpha)}(2j).$$  |  | (12)
L147: 
L148: We say that a specific global charge $Q^{(\alpha)}$ is conserved, if
L149: 
L150:  | $$Q^{(\alpha)}=Q^{(\alpha)}\circ\mathcal{V}$$  |  | (13)
L151: 
L152: in every volume $L\geq\alpha$, such that the charge density $q^{(\alpha)}$ is not changed as we increase $L$. The same definition applies for charges of the form (cite83†12 ).
L153: Formulas (cite84†8 )-(cite85†9 ) are immediately generalized to the quantum case. Regarding the charges, in the quantum case one deals with local operator densities $\hat{q}^{(\alpha)}$ and global charge operators $\hat{Q}^{(\alpha)}$ and the value of a given charge on a state ${\left|\Psi\right\rangle}$ is given by the mean value ${\left\langle\Psi\right|}\hat{Q}^{(\alpha)}{\left|\Psi\right\rangle}$. A quantum charge is conserved if it commutes with the time evolution as an operator:
L154:  | $$\hat{Q}^{(\alpha)}\hat{\mathcal{V}}=\hat{\mathcal{V}}\hat{Q}^{(\alpha)}.$$  |  | (14)
L155: If the quantum circuit is deterministic, and if we restrict ourselves to states ${\left|\Psi\right\rangle}$ which are product states in our computational basis, then the statement (cite86†13 ) is equivalent to the conservation of ${\left\langle\Psi\right|}\hat{Q}^{(\alpha)}{\left|\Psi\right\rangle}$ which follows from (cite87†14 ). However, the commutativity (cite87†14 ) carries more information than the classical conservation law, which is stored in the off-diagonal elements of the relation.
L156: In the quantum setting ballistically propagating one-site operators were studied in [cite88†53 ], they were called “solitons”. In Clifford automata ballistically propagating multi-site charges were studied in [cite73†45 ] and they were called “gliders”.
L157: Let us now also define a concrete basis for the local charges in the classical setting. For one-site charges $X\to\mathbb{Z}$ let $[a]$ denote the characteristic function of the local state $a$. To be more precise the value of charge $[a]$ on a local variable $s\in X$ is
L158: 
L159:  | $$[a](s)=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }s=a\\
L160: 0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}$$  |  | (15)
L161: This definition gives $N-1$ independent one-site charges, because $\sum_{a=1}^{N}[a]=1$, where now $1$ stands for the constant map $X\to\mathbb{Z}$ whose value is $1\in\mathbb{Z}$.

L170: 
L171: We consider cellular automata, where the update rules are solutions to the set theoretical Yang-Baxter equation. We will focus mainly on $2\to 2$ models and we briefly discuss $3\to 1$ models in Section cite22†6 . L172: The set theoretical Yang-Baxter equation was introduced by Drinfeld in [cite65†37 ]. It is a relation for maps $U:X^{2}\to X^{2}$, which takes the form
L173: 
L174:  | $$U_{12}U_{23}U_{12}=U_{23}U_{12}U_{23}.$$  |  | (17)

Usually it is also required that $U^{2}=1$, although non-involutive solutions were also considered in the literature, see for example [cite67†39 ].

L254: ## II Exactly solved full counting statistics
L255: ### II.1 Time integrated current
L256: 
L257: We shall consider the total charge which is transferred between the left and right half of the system (through the origin $\ell=0$) in time $2t$ (after $t$ full time steps)
L258: 
L259:  | $$\mathrm{J}(t)=\sum_{\ell>0}\mathrm{q}^{2t}_{\ell}-\sum_{\ell>0}\mathrm{q}^{0}_{\ell}.$$  |  | (12)
L260: 
L261: This is exactly equal to the the time integrated current
L262:  | $$\mathrm{J}(t)=\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t-1}\mathrm{j}_{0}^{2t^{\prime}}=\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{2t-1}(-1)^{t^{\prime}+1}\mathrm{q}_{0}^{t^{\prime}},$$  |  | (13)
L263: 
L264: where $\mathrm{j}$ is the local current that satisfies a pair (due to even-odd staggering) of continuity relations
L265:  | $$\mathrm{q}_{2\ell}^{2t+2}-\mathrm{q}_{2\ell}^{2t}+\mathrm{j}_{2\ell+1}^{2t+1}-\mathrm{j}_{2\ell}^{2t}=0,\qquad\mathrm{q}_{2\ell+1}^{2t+2}-\mathrm{q}_{2\ell+1}^{2t}+\mathrm{j}_{2\ell+2}^{2t}-\mathrm{j}_{2\ell+1}^{2t+1}=0.$$  |  | (14)
L266:

L270: ### II.2 Exact moment generating function
L271: 
L272: Our aim is to compute the moment generating function (MGF)
L273: 
L274:  | $$G(\lambda|t)\equiv\langle e^{\lambda\mathrm{J}(t)}\rangle\equiv\sum_{\mathrm{J}}\mathcal{P}(\mathrm{J}|t)e^{\lambda\mathrm{J}},$$  |  | (16)
L275: 
L276: where $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ is the counting field and $\langle\bullet\rangle$ denotes the average over an invariant separable measure of initial configurations $\mathrm{q}_{\ell}\equiv\mathrm{q}_{\ell}^{0}$
L277:  | $$\mathbb{P}(\{\mathrm{q}_{\ell}\})=\prod_{\ell}p(\mathrm{q}_{\ell}),\qquad p(\pm)=\rho\frac{1\pm b}{2},\qquad p(\emptyset)=\bar{\rho}=1-\rho,$$  |  | (17)
L278: 
L279: with $0\leq\rho\leq 1$ the density of particles, $-1\leq b\leq 1$ the charge bias of the particles and $\overline{\rho}$ the density of vacancies. For later convenience we also introduce
L280: 
L281:  | $$\varDelta^{2}=\rho\overline{\rho}\in[0,1/4].$$  |  | (18)
L282: The idea is now to evaluate the average (cite159†16 ) in a nested way - an outer average over all relevant charge-less (neutral) particle configurations $\{\Sigma\}$, $\Sigma\subset\mathbb{Z}$, and an inner average, with a frozen particle configuration $\Sigma$, over all combinations of charges $\bigl\{\mathrm{q}_{\ell}\in\{+1,-1\}\bigr\}_{\ell\in\Sigma}$. Let us tag a particle starting from the initial configuration and follow its worldline.
L283: Note that distinct worldlines by definition of the dynamics cannot cross. Let $\Lambda_{\pm}\subset\Sigma$ denote the coordinates of initial particles, which after $t$ time-steps (i.e., at time $2t$) end on the opposite side of the lattice, i.e. passing from the interval $[-\infty,0]$ to $[1,\infty]$ for $\Lambda_{-}$ and the opposite for $\Lambda_{+}$. Note that due to non-crossing of worldlines, at most one of the subsets $\Lambda_{\pm}$ can be non-empty (see Fig. cite160†4 for an illustration).
L284: Considering the defining expression for the transported charge (cite161†12 ), an unbiased averaging over the measure (cite162†17 ) given a fixed occupancy configuration $\Sigma$ yields
L285:  | $$G(\lambda|t;\Sigma)=\prod_{\ell\in\Lambda_{-}}\langle e^{\lambda q_{\ell}}\rangle\prod_{\ell\in\Lambda_{+}}\langle e^{-\lambda q_{\ell}}\rangle=\mu_{-}^{|\Lambda_{-}|}\mu_{+}^{|\Lambda_{+}|},$$  |  | (19)
L286: 
L287: where
L288: 
L289:  | $$\mu_{\pm}=\cosh\lambda\mp b\sinh\lambda,$$  |  | (20)
L290: 
L291: and $|\Lambda_{\pm}|\equiv\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda_{\pm}}1$.
